stories.headline: Kenya reports 8th Ebola case as Congo outbreak expands across borders
stories.bodyText:
Kenya confirmed its eighth Ebola case on Sunday after another person tested positive while in quarantine. Meanwhile, the outbreak in Congo spread to an eighth province, raising concerns over further cross-border transmission across the region.
Kenya’s director-general for health, Patrick Amoth, said that a 49-year-old patient attendant had tested positive while in quarantine after being identified as a contact of the country’s first case.
"Today, 38 people were tested, and one tested positive for Ebola," Amoth said in an interview with Kenya’s Citizen TV.
"He is a 49-year-old man who is not a healthcare worker. He developed fever, headache and muscle pain."
According to Reuters, the man had attended to Kenya’s first Ebola patient, a 40-year-old Kenyan who travelled from DR Congo through Uganda and arrived in Kenya on October 3. The patient died at a Nairobi hospital on October 5.
Amoth said the latest patient had cleaned utensils and linens and was probably exposed to the first case. A health ministry source said he developed symptoms on Saturday and was isolated before testing positive on Sunday.
Three close relatives of the first patient and three health workers have also tested positive. Authorities identified around 130 contacts following the initial death, with 128 remaining in quarantine. Six other patients were reported to be stable after receiving supportive treatment.
Meanwhile, DR Congo’s health ministry confirmed two cases, including one death, in Nord-Ubangi province, which borders the Central African Republic. The development marks the outbreak’s spread to an eighth province, the Associated Press (AP) reported.
Authorities have recorded at least 9,400 cases and more than 4,500 deaths since the outbreak was declared in mid-May, making it the deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country’s history.
"We see pockets of Ebola generally going down, but unfortunately geographically it’s spreading out," World Health Organization Regional Director for Africa Mohamed Yakub Janabi told AP.
Janabi identified reluctance among infected people to seek medical care as a major challenge, with some deaths occurring in communities outside health facilities.
"Ebola is a community disease. If the community does not cooperate, it will be very difficult," epidemiologist Serge Ngalebato said.
Kenya has strengthened border screening, designated a gate at Nairobi’s main airport for flights from 10 high-risk countries and established an emergency hotline. Tanzania has also tightened screening and introduced 21-day monitoring for travellers from high-risk countries.

stories.headline: Oil prices ease as Trump waives Russia sanctions, Middle East risks persist
stories.deck: Oil prices have seen a downturn due to US President Donald Trump's decision to lift sanctions on Russia, causing worries about supply stability. Brent crude is now at $108.3 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate has decreased to $101.2 per barrel. Heightened security risks in the Middle East and the ongoing uncertainty of US-Iran talks are adding to the market's instability.
stories.bodyText:
Oil prices fell on Monday as US President Donald Trump’s decision to waive sanctions and tariffs on Russia raised the prospect of additional fuel supplies entering the market. However, continuing security threats in the Middle East and uncertainty over US-Iran negotiations kept the outlook for crude volatile.
Brent crude declined $1.56, or 1.42%, to $108.3, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude was down 0.25, or 0.25%, at $101.2 a barrel.
The previous week, US President Donald Trump had signed an executive order granting a waiver on key sanctions and tariffs imposed under the law known as the Graham Act. The legislation was signed last month after lawmakers urged the president to put pressure on Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
Secretary of state Marco Rubio said Trump would use up to 60 days to evaluate the economic consequences of the waiver.
The move came after Trump reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to export diesel to the US. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy criticised the US actions, saying they would hurt Ukraine.
Brent crude had climbed to $110 a barrel briefly on Friday, marking its first such level since May, as mounting tensions in the Middle East heightened concerns about the security of shipping routes and the availability of global energy supplies.
The pressure on supplies has been compounded by attacks on commercial vessels. Gulf crude flows fell to approximately 8.5 million barrels per day on a seven-day average last week, down from more than 20 million barrels per day in the previous week, according to analytics firm Kpler. In a note issued on Friday, the firm also reported at least 10 confirmed incidents involving commercial vessels during the week.
The risk of a wider regional confrontation remained in focus, with Egypt stating that it was prepared to offer Saudi Arabia the support required to protect its security and stability against Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis.
Despite Monday’s decline, crude markets face another week of potential price swings. Supply concerns across West Asia and stalled negotiations between the US and Iran are fuelling fears of further disruptions, while measures aimed at easing shortages are providing some relief, analysts said.
Market participants will look to upcoming inventory figures for a clearer picture of supply and demand. The data under scrutiny include weekly crude stock estimates from the American Petroleum Institute (API), inventories at Cushing, total US oil stocks and crude imports.
Developments around the Strait of Hormuz will also remain crucial to the market outlook. Any interruption to shipments through the strategic waterway could further restrict global oil supplies, adding to the uncertainty surrounding prices.

stories.headline: Russian military satellite makes ‘close approach’ to U.S. radar satellite in orbit
stories.deck: Russia’s Cosmos-2612 satellite has changed its orbit repeatedly to approach ICEYE-X36, a commercial radar-imaging satellite registered in the U.S. and whose operator currently supplies data to Ukraine
stories.bodyText:
Russia and Ukraine are at war on the ground — and two satellites around 550 km above have come to the centre of a similar confrontation. The Russian Cosmos-2612 satellite has changed its orbit repeatedly to approach ICEYE-X36, a commercial radar-imaging satellite registered in the U.S. and whose operator currently supplies radar data to Ukraine.
While no attack of any kind had been established as of 10 am IST on October 18, astronomer and TU Delft lecturer Marco Langbroek had estimated late on the previous day that the two satellites were only 1-2 km apart — considered a very small distance in earth orbit — and expected them to get within metres of each other if their existing trajectories continued.

stories.headline: France protests: Macron vows to hold accountable those who ‘sought to bring down the Republic’
stories.deck: Macron blamed “unrestrained violence” on “insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals”
stories.bodyText:
French President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday (October 18, 2026) voiced the public's “anger” and “shame” over rioting and looting during nationwide protests against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. At least 1,800 people have been arrested.
“Those who looted will have to pay back for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable,” Mr. Macron said in a televised address to the nation.
He blamed “unrestrained violence” on “insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals.”
Mr. Macron has earlier held an emergency meeting with senior government officials, a day after masked groups set fires and attacked public buildings, including city halls, in several cities. He said he had instructed prefects to work with Mayors to protect public buildings and businesses in the coming weeks, including by banning protests when necessary.
Flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall in the city of Limoges, in central France, causing its roof to collapse and nearly destroying the building.
Hundreds of protesters gathered again on Sunday (October 18, 2026) at the Place de la République in Paris amid a heavy police presence. Officers used tear gas as tensions flared sporadically in the neighbourhood, with small groups of people trying to set bicycles and trash bins on fire.
“The right to protest is a fundamental right. Deliberately and collectively sowing disorder through violence is not,” Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez wrote on X, citing the looting of hundreds of businesses in cities including Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux.
About 5,50,000 people took part in protests across France, according to authorities, while organisers put the figure at about 8,00,000. Demonstrators answered calls from a labour union, student organisations and activists hoping to revive the “yellow vest” movement, which emerged in 2018 to protest social injustice.
Mass protests in France are often marred by violence on the fringes of otherwise peaceful marches, leading to clashes with police. The arrest tally reported Sunday (October 18, 2026) approached the nearly 2,000 recorded nationwide during a single day of yellow vest protests in December 2018.
One person died of a heart attack, Paris police said in a statement, without providing details. The Paris prosecutor's office said it was investigating.
Parisians deplore shattered shops and a damaged square
Dislodged cobblestones, shattered storefronts and broken glass littered the area around Paris' Place de la République on Sunday (October 18, 2026). Looting and damage were also reported in other tourist and shopping districts.
Paris police said 855 people were arrested in the capital region. The city's prosecutor's office said 557 remained in police custody.
“I am actually stunned by the level of destruction and violence that was expressed,” said government employee Marie Peyreigne, 57, wondering what had led to the mayhem.
Parisians inspecting the damage photographed the partially dismantled base of the square's central monument, a statue of Marianne, a symbol of France.
Jean Foissy, 74, said he had wanted to join the protest but encountered “a wall of riot police and fires everywhere” and returned home.
“I was very scared,” he said. “I've been a Parisian since I was born, so when I got here, it almost made me want to cry because I find it so bad, it hurts me.”
Margaux Eude, 26, said she supported the protest movement but “didn't think it would escalate like this.”
“It's the troublemakers who came, and it breaks my heart because it delegitimises the movement,” she said.
Political leaders trade blame ahead of presidential election
Political leaders across the spectrum sought to parlay the fallout of Saturday's (October 17, 2026) riots into political capital, looking ahead to next spring's presidential election.
Far-right leader and presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen criticized Macron's centrist government as “exhausted, disoriented and seemingly incapable of doing anything other than commenting on its own powerlessness,” in a video posted Sunday on social media.
Far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, for his part, accused Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu of “playing with fire,” alleging that “by banking on degradation, you have only succeeded in uniting all youths and workers' unions.”
Mr. Mélenchon, who joined the Paris march Saturday, insisted that “my message is clear: those who share our fight have no business in looting or destruction.”
U.S. President Donald Trump posted “France is burning!” on his Truth Social platform, apparently linking the unrest to “the immigration of people from an entirely different world.”
“Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!” he wrote.
French authorities and police have not linked immigrants to the rioting and have repeatedly attributed some of the violence to “radical far-left groups” and other people who joined to loot.
Published - October 19, 2026 07:00 am IST

Temple development works worth ₹2,500 crore under way across Telangana: Bhatti Vikramarka
briefs.bodyText:
The State government is spending around ₹2,000 crore on developing temples along the Godavari and riverbank areas ahead of the Godavari Pushkaralu scheduled for next year, Deputy Chief Minister Mallu Bhatti Vikramarka said on Sunday.
He said ₹276 crore had been allocated for the development of Sri Sitaramachandra Swamy temple at Bhadrachalam and ₹354 crore for the Sri Gnana Saraswati temple at Basar.
In all, temple development works were being undertaken across the State at an estimated cost of ₹2,500 crore, he added.
Mr. Vikramarka was speaking after laying the foundation stone for a road at an estimated cost of ₹44 crore at Nacharam village in Enkoor mandal of Khammam district. He also offered prayers at the Adbhutha Venkateswara Swamy temple in the village.
He said the road would ensure easier access for devotees and create employment and livelihood opportunities for local youth.
Highlighting the Congress government’s welfare initiatives, he said fine rice was being distributed to 1.06 crore families, while Rajiv Aarogyasri provided free medical treatment of up to ₹10 lakh per family. Rythu Bharosa assistance was being extended to 71 lakh farmers, and 53 lakh families were receiving free electricity for consumption of up to 200 units a month.
Other initiatives included interest-free loans to women, social security pensions for eligible beneficiaries, free bus travel for women and Indiramma houses for the poor, he said.
In the education sector, the State government was implementing a breakfast scheme for 27 lakh students of government schools, establishing Advanced Technology Centres and taking up construction of Young India Integrated Residential Schools in every Assembly constituency at an estimated cost of ₹200 crore.
The government was also undertaking road development works worth ₹90,000 crore across the State and taking steps to ensure uninterrupted power supply despite electricity demand exceeding 20,000 MW, he said.
Referring to the potential impact of El Nino, Mr. Vikramarka urged people to conserve water and appealed to farmers to monitor groundwater levels and use agricultural pumps judiciously.

briefs.headline: IUML Keralam chief Sadikali Thangal downplays row over Waqf board reconstitution
briefs.deck: Syed Sadikali Shihab Thangal says that at all Muslim organisations have been given representation in the board and those left out could be considered for membership in other bodies
briefs.bodyText:
Indian Union Muslim League (IUML) State president Syed Sadikali Shihab Thangal on Sunday downplayed the controversy over the reconstitution of the State Waqf Board.
He told the media here that those who had grievances were free to approach the court. Mr. Thangal maintained that all Muslim organisations had been given representation in the board and those left out could be considered for membership in other bodies.
“The bodies such as the Hajj Committee and the Madrasa Welfare Fund Board are yet to be reconstituted by the government. Those who have not been included in the Waqf board will be considered for such bodies,” Mr. Thangal said.
Amid criticism
His comments come against the backdrop of the criticism from the Samastha Kerala Jamiyyathul Ulama faction led by Sunni scholar Kanthapuram A.P. Aboobacker Musliar that they had not been given fair representation in the board.
Responding to allegations that Sunni organisations managing a large number of Waqf properties, such as the Kanthapuram faction, had been denied proper representation, Mr. Thangal said the board would address all these concerns without any discrimination. He said the chairman of the Hajj Committee is still a representative of the Kanthapuram faction and that the United Democratic Front (UDF) government did not change that arrangement.
He also maintained that the reconstituted Waqf board included representatives associated with the Samastha. “There are two representatives from the Samastha. One is the chairman himself, who is among its prominent members. Musthafal Faisy is also from the Samastha,” Mr. Thangal said.

briefs.headline: Elaborate arrangements made for Teppotsavam in Vijayawada on October 20
briefs.deck: Police personnel and expert swimmers deployed at bathing ghats along the Krishna River; the float festival was cancelled in 2025 and 2024 due to floods
briefs.bodyText:
Elaborate arrangements are being made for the Teppotsavam (float festival), the concluding ceremony of the nine-day Dasara Navaratri celebrations of the Kanaka Durga temple atop Indrakeeldari in Vijayawada, in the Krishna River on October 20.
Devotees are excited for the Teppotsavam this year as it was cancelled in the last two years due to the floods in the Krishna.
Officials of endowments, police, irrigation and other departments are making elaborate arrangements for the boat ride of Goddess Kanaka Durga and Lord Malleswara Swamy.
The Hamsa Vahanam, on which the deities will take a ride on the Krishna river, has been decked up.
The officials conducted a trial run of the Hamsa Vahanam (boat) on Sunday.
The police have deployed personnel on the ghats as a precautionary measure and the Irrigation Department has deployed expert swimmers at the bathing ghats.
The Hamsa Vahanam and the Durga and Punnami ghats have been illuminated for the festival.
The NTR Commissionerate Police will take the deities in a procession along the Brahmana Veedhi. Shami Puja and Paruveta will also be performed in Jammidoddi as part of the rituals.

briefs.headline: Two held for sexual exploitation of minor of minor in Kovalam spa
briefs.bodyText:
The Thiruvananthapuram City Police have arrested two men in connection with the alleged exploitation of a 16-year-old girl at a spa in Kovalam.
The Kovalam police identified the accused persons as Nishanth, 46, of Poovar, and Sajith Kumar, 47, of Mavelikkara.
The victim, a native of Andhra Pradesh, is suspected to have been brought to Kovalam in July by her maternal aunt and the aunt’s husband, who were responsible for her care after her parents’ death.
The investigators suspect that the relatives used forged documents to falsely establish that the girl was 20 years old. An Aadhaar card in her possession, which indicated that age, was found to be fake, according to the police.
The girl had purportedly been working at various spas since July and was subjected to sexual exploitation. Her ordeal came to light after she reportedly fell in love with a man at one of the spas and attempted to flee. She disclosed details of the alleged abuse during counselling.
The girl’s relatives, who are accused of trafficking and exploiting her, are believed to have returned to Andhra Pradesh. The Kovalam police have launched an investigation to trace them.
Meanwhile, the City police are pursuing the suspected involvement of a health official in the operations of a spa. Leads of possible benami transactions emerged during an examination of Nishanth’s mobile phone, an official said.
In wake of the incident, the Kerala Police conducted a Statewide crackdown on spas and wellness centres. centers. The police inspected 586 spas and registered 14 cases for various violations. Five persons were taken into custody during the raid. Besides, as many as 44 spas that operate in violation of statutory regulations have been served notices.

briefs.headline: 60-day pause on Russia sanctions to analyse global impact: Rubio
briefs.deck: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the waiver from sanctions on Russia and tariffs on other countries, including India, was a 60-day pause to analyse the global impact of the measure.
briefs.bodyText:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the waiver from sanctions on Russia and tariffs on other countries, including India, was a 60-day pause to analyse the global impact of the measure.
Mr. Rubio was responding to questions on Saturday at Joint Base Andrews near here as he left for a six-day tour of Uzbekistan and India.
“I think the President wants to take the 60 days to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy, and even to the U.S. economy,” Mr. Rubio said in response to a question on the waivers granted by Mr. Trump under the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act or the Graham Act.
On Friday (October 16, 2026), Mr. Trump waived key provisions of the Graham Act that authorised punitive tariffs on countries purchasing Russian oil, offering relief to India.
The executive order states that the waivers will remain in effect until the President or the Secretary of State, in consultation with the Secretary of the Treasury and the Trade Representative, as appropriate, determine that further action is appropriate.
Speaking to reporters at Mar-a-Lago resort near Miami, Mr. Trump said his decision to waive sanctions under the Graham Act would benefit the U.S.
“A lot of you don't know what my decision is yet, but we'll figure it out, and you'll figure it out,” he said.
“It's a very good decision, and it's going to be a decision that's good for the country, and I think good for the world because we're really at a world stage,” Mr. Trump said.
Mr. Rubio said when the Graham Act was passed, the waivers were put in to study the different things going around the world such as the pressure on global energy supplies due to the Iran war, the attack of Houthis in Saudi Arabia and the Ukraine-Russia war.
“So I think you have to take all of that into account and weigh it against each other,” Mr. Rubio said.
“Then you've got countries like India, for example, that have voluntarily diversified their energy portfolio, but are still getting a substantial amount of energy from Russia because it's hard to pivot from one day to the next,” said the Secretary of State, who is scheduled to be in India on Monday (October 19).
‘Key ally of U.S.’
Mr. Rubio said India was an important ally and partner of the United States, and the President needed that period of time to study all this and figure out what the right combination was.
Mr. Trump’s decision to waive sanctions on Russia came under fire from the Republicans and Democrats, who last month came together to overwhelmingly pass the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act.
Senator Darline Graham, a Republican from South Carolina, also criticised Mr. Trump for exempting Russia from a sanctions law that was championed by and named after her late brother Lindsey.
“Personally, I would choose to put the pressure on Russia to end the war and get gas prices down, because I don’t trust [President Vladimir] Putin, and I don’t trust Russia,” said Ms. Graham, who was endorsed by Mr. Trump to fill in the Senate seat that fell vacant due to the death of her brother.
“Beyond irresponsible,” said Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, on social media.
“What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand,” Mr. Tillis said.
“It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine,” he said.
Mr. Tillis said if Mr. Trump wanted to actually bring down energy prices, he should resolve the Iran war, which was largely blamed for the spike at the pump, and not do a solid for Mr. Putin.
Republican Senator John Cornyn of Texas said, “Lindsey would be appalled,” referring to the late Senator Lindsey Graham, who worked endlessly on the bill before he died this summer.
Senator Elizabeth Warren, Democrat from Massachusetts, said Trump was thumbing his nose at Congress and enabling Mr. Putin to continue his war of aggression. She urged her colleagues to take action to reverse course.
Published - October 18, 2026 08:18 am IST

briefs.headline: Vadaanya Talent Test 2026 to be held in Anantapur, Sri Sathya Sai districts on December 13
briefs.bodyText:
Vadaanya Janaa Society, an NGO established in 2010 to support underprivileged and talented students from rural areas, will be organising the Vadaanya Talent Test 2026 on December 13, 2026, in Anantapur and Sri Sathya Sai districts of Andhra Pradesh.
The announcement was made during a programme held at AF Ecology Centre, Anantapur, where the Vadaanya Talent Test 2026 poster and question booklet were released. Necessary permissions for the conduct of the examination were obtained from the respective District Collectors and District Education Officers, Vadaanya founder Ashok Padapati said.
As part of its preparations for the 2026 examination, Vadaanya released the question booklet containing question papers from the previous five years. The booklet aims to help students understand the examination pattern and prepare effectively.
The organisers expect approximately 10,000 students from government schools across the two districts to participate. Online registrations would begin on November 1, 2026. Registration details, eligibility criteria, and examination updates can be found on the website: www.vadaanya.org.
Established in 2010, Vadaanya Janaa Society has been working to improve educational opportunities for rural students through scholarships, mentoring, academic support, and talent identification initiatives. Over the years, the organisation has supported and guided thousands of students in pursuing their educational goals.
Several students identified through Vadaanya’s Talent Test have achieved good results in competitive examinations such as JEE Main and secured admissions to prestigious institutions, including IITs and IISc Bengaluru.
Y. V. Mallareddy of AF Ecology Centre and other guests attended the programme and appreciated Vadaanya’s efforts to promote education among rural students.
The examination aims to identify talented students who have studied in government schools up to Class 10 and provide them with guidance and encouragement to pursue higher education at leading institutions such as IITs, NITs, and IISc.
Published - October 18, 2026 07:51 pm IST

briefs.headline: Karnataka revises penalties for officials, false grievances under new Act
briefs.bodyText:
Under the Karnataka Sakala Services (Amendment) Act, 2026, the State government has revised financial penalties for defaulting officials as well as citizens filing frivolous or malicious grievances.
Under the amended provisions, officials who fail to deliver services or dispose of appeals within the stipulated timeframe will face financial penalties, which will be deducted directly from their salaries and awarded as compensation to the applicant.
The penalty slab begins at ₹20 per day for the first one to five days of delay (capped at ₹100). This scales up to ₹100 per day for delays between 21 and 25 days, with a maximum cumulative penalty of ₹1,500. Additionally, for deficient service or wrongful rejection of applications without valid grounds, a penalty of up to ₹1,500 will be recovered from the responsible officer, according to the notification.
To curb misuse of the grievance mechanism, the Amendment empowers authorities to penalise citizens who file false or malicious complaints intended to harass or intimidate government personnel. If an inquiry confirms that a complaint was filed with ulterior motives, the applicant will be fined ₹1,500 per application, with repeat offences attracting an additional fine of ₹1,500 per instance, recoverable as arrears of land revenue.
Published - October 18, 2026 07:49 pm IST

stories.headline: Law itself a living conversation: CJI Surya Kant
stories.deck: Earlier, the convocation was postponed after students and alumni of NLSIU, Bengaluru, came out in support of students at NALSAR, Hyderabad, opposing CJI Surya Kant at the convocation over his remarks on the youth of the country
stories.bodyText:
Chief Justice of India (CJI) and Chancellor of National Law School of India University (NLSIU), Bengaluru, Surya Kant, delivering the 34th convocation of NLSIU on Saturday (October 17, 2026), said the purpose of legal education “rests in the invigorating experience of encountering those who see the world differently than we do.”
Earlier, the convocation, which was scheduled to be held on September 12, was postponed after students and alumni of NLSIU, Bengaluru, came out in support of students at NALSAR, Hyderabad, opposing CJI Surya Kant at the convocation over his remarks on the youth of the country. His remarks in open court, which he clarified later, sparked the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) movement. However, the convocation held on October 17 went off peacefully, with no protests or any untoward incidents.
Law a living conversation
Elaborating on the idea of law as encountering different points of view, Justice Surya Kant said, “Within the halls, we sit beside people whose backgrounds, beliefs, and interpretations challenge our own. Each time we listen to perspectives that diverge from ours, we are reminded that the law itself is a living conversation, shaped by voices that do not always harmonise, but together create the symphony of justice. It is your relentless pursuit of honesty which will cement your professional reputation.”
Asking the students to uphold the Constitution and its values, he said, “Law will change your patience, test your ethics, and call upon the deepest reserves of your courage, but it will also reward you with a singular joy of service, the serene satisfaction of righting a wrong, the pride of defending liberty, and the honour of upholding the Constitution.”
“The cases you are on, the contracts you brought, the advice you give at the judgments you write, will all contribute to the larger architecture of justice in our nation,” he said, telling students that as they left the campus, they “step not only into profession, but into a calling to be guardians of autonomy and servants of the people.”
Published - October 17, 2026 05:39 pm IST

stories.headline: ‘Cabinet decision on Bangalore Turf Club land for High Court this month’
stories.bodyText:
Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar announced that the State Cabinet will decide later this month on allocating land for the new building of the High Court of Karnataka “on the Race Course premises”. He was speaking at the foundation stone laying ceremony of the NLSIU South Campus at Nagarbhavi in Bengaluru on Saturday.
“I have been receiving requests from the Chief Justice of the High Court of Karnataka for alternate building. It is the only High Court in India that is facing the legislature house. So we are planning for a new building. We will speed up the process of allocation of land. It will be build on 12-15 acres of land,” he said, adding he wished Justice Surya Kant will also lay the foundation stone for the new building by the end of his tenure.
Filing an affidavit in response to a Public Interest Litigation (PIL), the Karnataka Government had in July, 2026, informed the High Court that it will soon pass a resolution allocating the BTC land for construction of a new high court building. Earlier in the year, in February, 2026, the cabinet had approved the relocation plan of BTC races to Kunigal Stud Farm in Tumakuru. BTC has also agreed to shift its operations, racing out of the city, sources said.
NLSIU South campus
The Chief Minister laid the foundation stone for the new NLSIU South Campus which will be built on 7 acres of land allotted by the Karnataka Government. This will include 2000 student rooms and 90 units of faculty and staff residences. NLSIU also plans to build a new auditorium, student centre and research facilities on the existing campus site.
Meanwhile Mr. Shivakumar announced that the government will start a coaching institute to provide training for judicial service examinations to law graduates and offer continuing education for young lawyers. He said while there were many coaching institutes for other entrance exams, there were none for law aspirants.
Never stop questioning, CM tells law students
Chief Minister D. K. Shivakumar exhorted students graduating out of the National Law School of India University, Bengaluru, to “never stop questioning”, in the presence of the Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, on October 17, 2026, Saturday. He warned that if students don’t question then it will pave an easy way for people in power or others to decide for them.
“To protect democratic institutions, uphold constitutional values, and ensure justice for every citizen—never stop questioning, never compromise on your values, and never forget the people,” he said. “A robust democracy must provide citizens with the opportunity to question the government. At a time when democratic institutions across the world are facing challenges, young lawyers and policymakers bear a special responsibility to protect the Constitution. A strong democracy is not one where everyone agrees with the government; rather, a truly robust democracy is one where every citizen possesses the freedom to question the government,” he added.
Law student awarded 15 gold medals
Manhar Bansal, a BA LLB (Hons) graduate received 15 gold medals for his achievements in academics at NLSIU. He is also the best Outgoing Undergraduate Student and secured first rank in the University and in various individual subjects. In November 2025, he was awarded the Rhodes Scholarship for India 2026 on which he is currently pursuing Master of Studies in Comparative Literature and Critical Translation at Oxford University in the UK.
“I am originally from Punjab and was always fascinated with the humanities and the social sciences and therefore chose to pursue the law. The days at NLSIU were the most transformational years of my academic as well as personal life. I was part of an intellectual community of faculty and peers that pushed me to think fearlessly. After my time at Oxford, I intend to pursue a PhD in Comparative Literature and work towards a public-facing academic career,” he said.
Assam CM in the audience
Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma was among the audience at the NLSIU Bengaluru’s convocation on Saturday. His son Nandil Biswa Sarma was among the law graduates to receive degree on the convocation ceremony. Mr. Sarma and his family was present during the ceremony to see his son receive degree from CJI Surya Kant.
Published - October 18, 2026 12:54 am IST

stories.headline: Festive spirit drives weekend park volunteering in Bengaluru
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru: The spirit of 
Dasara
 found its way into the city’s neighbourhood parks over the weekend, as citizens came together for another round of activities under #IamBengaluru – Volunteer for Parks, presented by Multigen, in association with Kristu Jayanti University and supported by Greater Bengaluru Authority.
The weekend began with a de-weeding activity at Jakkur Lake Park, led by Jala Poshan, and a waste segregation and clean-up drive at BDA Doddakallasandra Park-2, organised by Youth for Seva. Volunteers braved the rain to keep the momentum going.
On Sunday, volunteers explored Bengaluru’s urban biodiversity through a nature walk and biodiversity survey at Rachenahalli Lake Park, led by Naturalist School. At Senior Citizens Park, JP Nagar 7th Phase, Women of Wisdom organised a community collection drive, bringing a spirit of sharing to the weekend.

The Times of India
 through #IamBengaluru gives us a wonderful platform to take this message to more citizens, especially the youth. Together, we can encourage people to understand the value of native plants and take greater ownership of the city’s parks.”

TOI

stories.headline: Bengaluru’s Kempegowda Metro station hosts immersive heritage art display
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 Shortly after Metro services were terminated Friday night, the platform walls of Nadaprabhu Kempegowda station in Majestic turned into a canvas displaying Karnataka’s mythical forms and cultural heritage.
The 16,000sqft visual experience was organised by an out-of-home (OOH) advertising company around 11.30pm. The midnight art soirée, titled ‘Stone to Life,’ used the Epson EB-L20000U Japanese projector, which delivers 20,000 lumens of brightness and WUXGA resolution. The projection mapping transformed the existing walls beneath platforms 3 and 4 into a canvas for cultural storytelling, bringing Karnataka’s mythical forms and temple heritage to life.
Curated by Team Gen O, Mumbai, the event put on canvas five mythical forms rooted in Karnataka’s architectural heritage: Yali, Vrishabha-Kunjara, Gandabherunda, Makara, and Kirtimukha. Historian Srinivas Sistla, associate professor in the department of fine arts, Andhra University, Visakhapatnam, spoke about the cultural and historical significance underpinning the immersive art experience.
Ads on platform walls
Bangalore Metro Rail Corporation Ltd has also entered into an agreement with the OOH firm to display projected ads on platforms 3 and 4 using the same technology. Shripad Ashtekar, managing director of Signpost India Ltd, stated that the future of ad-tech and digital advertising lies in rethinking the role public spaces play in a city’s everyday life.

briefs.headline: Protests, match and festivals bring Bengaluru traffic to a standstill
briefs.bodyText:
A mix of protests, sporting events and festivals paralysed Bengaluru, as the city was gridlocked on Saturday. Several key stretches, including J.C. Road, M.G. Road, Hosur Road and Tumakuru Road, were choked with outstation buses trying to leave the city.
On Saturday evening, several roads in Central Bengaluru were congested. The police had made barricading arrangements around M. Chinnaswamy Stadium for the India-West Indies match. This, coupled with rain, slowed traffic across the Central Bengaluru District. Parking restrictions further worsened the situation. Traffic gridlock in the Central Business District (CBD) continued even till almost midnight as the match was called off due to rain and spectators started leaving the stadium.
Around Nrupathunga Road, traffic was affected by Union Minister H.D. Kumaraswamy’s visit to the Director General of Police headquarters. Further, the police had made arrangements around J.C. Road, as the All India Students Association (AISA) had called for a protest near Town Hall. The barricades and arrangements for buses added to the congestion.
Outstation buses
Meanwhile, Tumakuru Road near Goraguntepalya was gridlocked, with inter-district buses lining up. Long queues of traffic were also reported near the exit point at Majestic.
Keerthana M., a Koramangala resident who was travelling to her hometown of Hassan, said the bus she was travelling in was stuck within the city for almost two hours, and the journey to her district took six hours. “I took the bus around 3 p.m., thinking I would get out in the evening traffic but couldn’t escape,” she said.
In the southern part of the city, commuters heading towards Chandapura were stuck in gridlock for more than three hours. Several took to social media to share their ordeal. However, many commuters claimed that travel on Friday night had been worse, with some taking over six hours to cross the city limits.
An X user wrote that it took four hours to cover the stretch from Silk Board to Attibele on Friday night. Traffic on Mysuru Road also crawled, with several car users taking to the road on Saturday.
Railway stations
City railway stations also witnessed an unusually large number of passengers. Manjunath, who boarded a train at SMVT station, said the entire station was a nightmare.
“The situation was really bad, with all passengers pushing each other. It was a packed situation,” he said.

briefs.headline: Stumps down, dandiya up: Bengaluru plays on
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru’s Saturday evening plans took an unexpected turn as rain swept across the city, triggering traffic snarls, cab woes and a washout at the M Chinnaswamy Stadium. The downpour tried to play spoilsport, but Garba lovers refused to let the showers dampen their festive spirit.
What happened?
Rain lashed Bengaluru on Saturday evening as the city geared up for Garba celebrations and sporting action. While commuters struggled to find cabs, cricket fans faced disappointment as the rain halted the much-awaited T20I decider.
Traffic: Soaring fares and a scramble for cabs
The downpour left commuters struggling to get around the city, with cab cancellations and soaring fares adding to their woes. Some AC cab fares reportedly touched ₹100 per kilometre, turning even a short ride into an expensive affair.
Garba: Rain-soaked, but still dancing
Garba venues across Bengaluru turned into a sea of umbrellas, with wet grounds and soaked outfits doing little to deter revellers. Instead of calling it a night, many chose to keep dancing through the downpour.
Videos and pictures shared on social media showed people performing Garba in the rain, turning an evening disrupted by the weather into an impromptu celebration. 
For many, the night became less about perfect steps and more about making memories.
Cricket: Rain washes out the decider
Cricket fans had little reason to cheer. The India-West Indies T20I series decider at the M Chinnaswamy Stadium was abandoned without a result after India made a strong start, recording their fastest men’s T20I fifty.
The rain brought the match to a halt, leaving fans without a finish to the contest and the five-match series tied 2-2.
The bigger picture: Bengaluru refuses to let the rain spoil the night
Saturday night was a study in contrasts: traffic chaos on the roads, disappointment at the stadium and an unexpected celebration on rain-soaked dance floors. The rain may have stopped the cricket, but Garba went on, one rain-soaked twirl at a time.

briefs.headline: NHAI begins work on long-delayed FOB after pedestrian deaths on Bengaluru–Mysuru highway
briefs.bodyText:
After more than four pedestrian deaths and several non-fatal accidents in 16 months, the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) has finally begun work to fix the black spot near the Kaniminike Toll Plaza on the Bengaluru-Mysuru Highway.
The black spot, spanning about 100 to 150 metres, is located about 600 metres from the Kaniminike Toll Plaza. More than 1,000 students use this stretch every day, as a private university is located about 100 metres from the black spot.
Paying guest accommodations
Sameer, a student at the university, explained that several paying guest accommodations are located on the other side of the highway, forcing many students to cross it at the black spot in the absence of a foot overbridge (FOB), putting their lives at risk. Meanwhile, work on constructing an FOB was taken up nearly 22 months ago but remained unfinished. The Hindu had recently reported about the issue.
“Many of us have witnessed deaths on this stretch, and for the next few days, we would dread crossing it. Seeing the work begin is a big relief,” he said.
Although pedestrians can use the Kaniminike Toll Plaza to cross the highway safely, they rarely take that route because doing so requires them to walk an additional kilometre.
According to the Bengaluru Traffic Police data, about four people have died at the black spot since January 2025, and more than 10 non-fatal accidents have been reported.
Shashank S., a local resident, said another non-fatal accident occurred earlier this week.
To be completed in 10 days
The contractor executing the work told The Hindu that the design had to be changed and slightly skewed after property owners raised concerns about the structure abutting their sites, causing a delay.
“It was challenging to change the structural design. We have assembled the substructures elsewhere and brought them to the location. Now, superstructure construction is underway,” he said.
The contractor assured that the work would be completed within a week and that the FOB could be opened to pedestrians within the next 10 days. He said land issues and exorbitant steel prices had forced them to postpone the work, which was supposed to resume in August.
After multiple complaints
The FOB remained unfinished for more than 22 months, forcing citizens to follow up regularly through letters. “Even after sending the letter, we had to follow up multiple times and push them to act. Now, the contractor is expediting the work,” Mr. Shashank said.
According to NHAI sources, land issues were the primary reason for the prolonged delay in executing the project.

briefs.headline: Karnataka SIR: 37 voters file Form-7 saying they are dead; 334 pairs declare each other dead
briefs.deck: Most forms declaring the applicant dead filed before SIR began, but at least three cases included in SIR draft rolls; poll officials cite software glitches, unexplained discrepancies
briefs.bodyText:
At least 37 people have reportedly filed forms seeking the deletion of their own names from Karnataka’s electoral rolls on the ground that they were “dead”. The name of the person filing the objection and the name to be deleted were the same, even including their initials, according to an analysis by The Hindu.
In another bizarre pattern, 334 pairs of people have declared each other dead. One person filed a Form-7 seeking deletion of the other’s name, citing death as the reason; the person declared dead then filed a similar form, declaring the first person dead as well.
In all cases, both people in each pair were listed at the same polling station, according to an analysis of Election Commission of India (ECI) data processed by Mandate Analytics and Consulting (MAC Insights).
Some cases included in draft rolls
Most of the forms in which people sought deletion of their own names, citing death as the reason, were filed before the special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls began across Karnataka on June 30. However, at least three such forms were filed even after the draft electoral rolls were published, meaning these names were also part of the draft rolls.
The Hindu checked these three cases with Booth Level Officers (BLOs) and Assistant Electoral Registration Officers (AEROs). The cases were reported in the Magadi, Sandur, and Byatarayanapura Assembly constituencies, with forms filed between September 17 and 26.
Unexplained discrepancies
In Byatarayanapura, Sudha K.N., 25, was listed as both the person filing Form-7 and the person whose name was sought to be deleted, with “dead” cited as the reason. However, the BLO told The Hindu that the form sought the deletion of an elector named Srikanth and had been filed by his wife, Sudha. But Srikanth’s name in the electoral rolls was listed as Sudha K.N., a discrepancy the BLO could not explain. The BLO said she was unaware whether this was a software glitch during the enumeration phase or whether the discrepancy existed in earlier electoral rolls.
In Sandur, Hanumantha, 30, filed a Form-7 seeking deletion of his own name, again citing death as the reason. Senior poll officials attributed the entry to a software glitch, while the BLO said she was unaware that a Form-7 had been filed.
In Magadi, Manish Gowda R. had filed the form. His serial number was listed as 416, but the draft electoral roll for the polling station concerned (Part No. 268) had only 415 electors.
Bizarre pairs peak in June
Meanwhile, the 334 pairs of electors who declared each other dead were spread across more than 25 districts. Belagavi accounted for the highest number of such cases, at 160, followed by Kalaburagi with 80, data processed by MAC Insights showed. While the cases were spread across multiple Assembly constituencies in these districts, all 28 such cases in Mysuru district were concentrated in the Chamundeshwari Assembly constituency. All were filed after the SIR was officially announced on May 14.
June saw the highest number of such cases, at 333. The electoral rolls were frozen on June 16, while the SIR exercise began across Karnataka on June 30. Most of these forms were filed before the SIR began in the State.
Mutual electoral destruction
The Hindu also
For instance, on May 17, in Raybag in Belagavi district, an elector named Gangubayi Vaddar sought the deletion of Rukmini Vaddar’s name, declaring her dead. On the same day, Rukmini Vaddar filed a form declaring Gangubayi Vaddar dead.
In another case, on June 8, in Nippani, an elector named Prabhakar Ranga Malage sought deletion of Malan Malage’s name, citing death as the reason. The next day, on June 9, Malan Malage, who had been declared dead a day earlier, sought deletion of Prabhakar Ranga Malage’s name, also citing death as the reason, the Form-10 report shows.
(With inputs from Pon Vasanth B.A., Chennai)

stories.headline: ‘We are learning to live with weaker currency’: Arvind Panagariya
stories.bodyText:
Columbia University professor and 16th Finance Commission chairman Arvind Panagariya, who was in India for the Kautilya Conclave, spoke to 
TOI
, arguing that a weaker rupee will not just make exports competitive but will also keep the prices of finished imported goods higher. In an interview, he suggested tariff cuts, doing away with quality control orders and revisiting bilateral investment treaties. 
Excerpts:Sitting in New York, how do you see the Indian economy evolving? What is the feedback that you’re getting from colleagues and investors?
The general perception of the Indian economy is very positive. My assessment is that we will continue to grow at 7-8%. Manufacturinggrowth of 10% or so in the last three years gives me a lot of confidence; it is a very positive sign for the future. Inflation has remained stable, current account deficit has been very manageable. So, the vitals are all good.
Given the headwinds due to west Asia in terms of higher cost, logistics, there is nervousness. Is that a big challenge?
I don’t see our entrepreneurs nervous about growth prospects. Headwinds have been there and entrepreneurs have learnt to live with these things. We emerged very quickly and robustly from Covid. Our exports to the US and overall went up despite Trump’s tariffs, which shows that exporters have learnt to cope with this uncertainty. 
Finally, we seem to also be learning that currency depreciation is not always a bad thing. It is a very important change in our own attitudes. Indian products have to be competitive in the domestic market compared to imported goods.
A big concern with a weaker rupee has been that import bill rises.
The increase in the cost of imports basically tells you that our goods are more competitive relative to the foreign goods. The cost of my inputs rises, but the cost of the goods that are coming in to compete with my (finished) goods rises even more. Our exports did so well between 2000 and 2011 because the dollar appreciated against the rupee between 1991 and 2002 by 170%. But it stayed around that level till 2011 or so, actually the rupee appreciated in nominal terms, before weakening. As a result, after crossing $300 billion in 2011-12, it fell below that mark and only increased post-Covid.
India has signed multiple trade agreements that reduce tariffs bilaterally. What else needs to be done?
This is much needed and I also want the agreement with the US to go through as it will not only give us access, it will also lead to the opening up of our own markets, which is very much required. Several QCOs have been suspended but there are many more that need to be repealed because they are offering protection. The Bureau of Indian Standards does not have the staff to implement them domestically and the intent seems to be protectionist. India is also among the top users of anti-dumping duty. Anti-dumping is sometimes even more pernicious than tariffs because these duties can be very large and also very targeted as you go after your cheapest supplier.
What about the bilateral investment treaty?
We need to take a comprehensive look at the bilateral investment treaties because if we are going to attract foreign investors then we have to see what our competitors are doing, what China is doing, what Vietnam is doing.
Do you see future American presidents weaponising tariffs the way Trump has done?
The US commitment to WTO has certainly weakened. The current President has acted as if WTO really doesn’t matter. The only restraint on him has been domestic US laws and even that he has at times neglected. I doubt if future presidents will do like that. But what has happened permanently, and is something that was already underway, is the weakening of the WTO discipline. Subsidies were given, like through the Chips Act during the Biden administration, which was in violation of WTO rules. With the appellate body not functioning there is no way it can be addressed.

stories.headline: ‘Call for digital swaraj reflects need for greater data control’: IBM India chief Sandip Patel
stories.bodyText:
MUMBAI: IBM India and South Asia managing director Sandip Patel said his call for “digital swaraj” reflects businesses’ and govts’ growing need to exercise greater control over their data, technology assets and the systems that manage them.
“I have started calling this the era of digital swaraj. In a predominantly digital world and a global digital economy, organisations need a degree of digital sovereignty suited to their level of regulation and the criticality of their operations,” Patel told TOI at its flagship event, IBM Think, held here.
Geopolitical developments and regulatory requirements have heightened concerns over data sovereignty, particularly among organisations in regulated sectors such as banking.
Companies increasingly want clarity on where their data resides and who controls encryption keys, where the control plane is located and whether compliance can be demonstrated continuously.
IBM’s Sovereign Core, announced in March, is designed to address these concerns. The software stack can be deployed in a client or partner-owned data centre, providing cloud-like capabilities while keeping control-plane operations and key management within the customer’s jurisdiction.
Built on Sovereign Core, IBM Bharat Core is an AI stack optimised for India, offering reusable Indic AI services, models and connectors across industries. It is benchmarked for quality and scale in Indian scenarios and guides users through the AI lifecycle by recommending suitable building blocks and infrastructure tailored to India’s requirements.
IBM is also developing India-specific tools to accelerate Sovereign Core implementation, while its Svaiam reference architecture is designed to help deploy sovereign AI capabilities within govt environments. The shift towards greater control over technology infrastructure is also supporting India’s data centre growth. Patel identified two drivers: companies building capacity in India to support global operations, and Indian enterprises investing in infrastructure they can control themselves.
IBM, MeitY Startup Hub to boost deep-tech ventures
IBM and MeitY Startup Hub (MSH), an initiative of the ministry of electronics and information technology, plan to accelerate India’s deep-tech startup ecosystem by providing startups access to IBM’s technology expertise, mentorship, enterprise engagement opportunities and skilling programmes. Startups will get access to IBM’s enterprise technologies and innovation platforms to address business use cases. These include IBM watsonx, an enterprise-ready AI and data platform and IBM Bob, an AI coding agent for enterprises.

stories.headline: Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford | Putting people in economics
stories.deck: The winners of the 2026 Economics Nobel Prize transformed macroeconomics by showing how individual choices, household expectations and business behaviour shape the economy and influence the effectiveness of government policies
stories.bodyText:
Most people view macroeconomics as a result of the mechanical tweaking of some variables to alter other variables. For example, if aggregate consumer demand is down, there is immediately a call for lower interest rates and higher government doles. Similarly, when demand outstrips supply, then the call is the opposite: raise interest rates and cut back on handouts.
There was also a long-held belief that unemployment and inflation had an inverse relationship — as shown in the famous Phillips Curve — and that income and consumption moved in tandem. If governments could tweak one, the belief was that this would result in changes in the other.
It was this that Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford turned on its head, for which they were awarded the 2026 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, commonly called the Economics Nobel. The economic thinking that the ‘invisible hand’ of the government should step in to stabilise the economy was born out of the landmark work of that titan of economic theory, John Maynard Keynes, and was put to great use in the aftermath of the Great Depression in the U.S. in the 1930s.
This stabilisation policy remained popular for several decades until it was upended by the oil shock the U.S. economy faced in the 1970s. During this crisis, the relationship between several macroeconomic variables broke down. That is, inflation rose at an accelerated pace even though unemployment was high, and the link between income and consumption looked like it was no longer holding.
What this meant was that conventional stabilisation policy no longer worked — government stimulus came at the wrong time, which had long-term detrimental effects on growth and inflation.
Economists such as Robert E. Lucas, the 1995 Economics Nobel Prize winner, then got to work to show that the dry mechanisms of simply working with macroeconomic variables were not the way. Inflation at the macro level was the result of pricing decisions by thousands of individual companies, and total private consumption was the result of actions taken by lakhs of individual households.
However, while it was increasingly accepted that households make consumption choices not only on the basis of their current situation but also on the basis of their future expectations, the difficulty arose in trying to quantify the effect of these future expectations.
Policy and behaviour
Enter Robert E. Hall. Born in 1943 in Palo Alto, California, Mr. Hall graduated from UC Berkeley in 1964 and earned his PhD from MIT. Even as a graduate student, he was already working on the issue of how government policy affects business behavior, research that eventually led to a seminal 1967 paper ‘Tax Policy and Investment Behavior’.
He went on to serve on the economics faculty of UC Berkeley from 1967 to 1970 before moving to MIT and then to Stanford University, where he still works as the Robert and Carole McNeil Joint Hoover Senior Fellow and Professor of Economics.
Mr. Hall’s greatest contribution, and for which he was awarded the Nobel Prize, however, had to do with the households not companies.
The central idea of his research, later put down in a landmark paper in 1978, was that if the consumption decisions of households is governed by their expectations of future income and other such factors, then their current consumption is also an accurate indicator of their future expectations. That is, if a household is optimistic about the future, it will consume more than if it were pessimistic.
A related observation was that households will also only ever change their consumption patterns if their assessment of the future changes. In turn, their assessment of the future changes when they obtain new and relevant information. Further, since new information cannot be predicted by definition, changes in consumption also cannot be predicted.
Now, here is the key for policymakers. If the rule is that changes in consumption cannot be predicted because they are based on unpredictable new information, then situations where it can be predicted must be because households are breaking this rule. This breaking of the rules usually takes place when a household is living paycheck to paycheck, or hand-to-mouth. They cannot borrow and have no savings, and so they spend only exactly what they earn. That is, their consumption is entirely predictable.
Using this finding, and the empirical work done by Mr. Hall, policymakers could now measure in exact terms the percentage of the population that was living hand-to-mouth.
The other major contribution of Mr. Hall’s work was bringing in a ‘human’ element to macroeconomics, providing policymakers a map of sorts to how individuals react to both fear and confidence about the future.
Mr. Hall’s work addressed the demand side, giving macroeconomics microeconomic underpinnings. The supply side theory was a result of the work done by Michael Woodford.
Mr. Woodford was born in 1955 in Massachusetts and he went on to complete his undergraduate studies at the University of Chicago, earn a Juris Doctor from Yale Law School, and complete his PhD in Economics from MIT. Not only did Mr. Woodford build on Mr. Hall’s demand side contributions, but he also brought about a decisive change in how inflation was viewed. That is, in a series of papers starting in the 1990s, he showed that inflation is based on the behaviour of individual companies that set prices, knowing that it would be too difficult to change these prices every time demand or input costs change. Firms are not only future-looking in their behaviour, but their prices also tend to be ‘sticky’ — they don’t change quickly.
Looking to the future
Now, the follow-up of this for policymakers was that, since businesses look to the future, their expectations about future interest rates are very important to manage inflation. As a result, it becomes of prime importance for central bank policies to be credible and transparent.
That is why the RBI Governor, while announcing interest rate decisions, puts them in the context of the global and Indian economies, and gives the rationale and outlook in detail. This policy of transparency is followed by all major central banks around the world and has its foundations in Mr. Woodford’s work.
Other aspects of Mr. Woodford’s work also provided policymakers more effective tools to deal with supply shocks than they had during the 1970s, such as using monetary policy to do the job rather than fiscal policy.
Mr. Woodford combined all of this with Mr. Hall’s demand side theory and created a complete framework, which he published in a 2003 monograph titled Making Things Happen: A Theory of Causal Explanation. This monograph laid the groundwork for understanding business cycles, what causes them, how they play out, their impact on stabilisation policy, and the importance of policy transparency.
In essence, the two economists provided the theoretical and empirical underpinnings to a basic but powerful idea for policymakers: the economy is made out of the people in it.

stories.headline: Indian refiners’ fuel exports to West surge 43% amid Russian crude imports
stories.deck: Reliance Industries Ltd.'s Jamnagar refinery in Gujarat supplied six of the seven cargoes unloaded at EU ports that month, despite the bloc's ban on fuel made from Russian crude
stories.bodyText:
Refineries in India and two other countries that run on Russian crude shipped 1 billion euros ($1.2 billion) of oil products to sanctioning countries in September, up 43% from August, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
Reliance Industries Ltd.'s Jamnagar refinery in Gujarat supplied six of the seven cargoes unloaded at EU ports that month, despite the bloc's ban on fuel made from Russian crude.
The CREA report covers refineries in India, Turkiye and Brunei. The EU took 667 million euros' worth of their products, Australia 168 million euros, the U.S. 154 million euros and New Zealand 19 million euros. CREA estimated 295 million euros' worth was refined from Russian crude.
Jamnagar also supplied the group's largest U.S.-bound exports, worth 122 million euros, and Russian crude made up 32% of its imports from July to September.
Italy received three of the seven EU-bound shipments, Romania two, and Spain and Cyprus one each. Exports reported as destined for EU ports from refineries running on Russian crude rose 80% in value, including a single 104,000-tonne cargo of gasoil (diesel) from Jamnagar still en route to Rotterdam.
The EU banned imports of oil products refined from Russian crude in January 2026. The ban exempts net crude exporters, but CREA says the exemption leaves a gap, since net-export status does not stop a country from refining Russian-origin crude. The report calls for applying the ban at the refinery level, barring products from any plant that has processed Russian crude in the previous six months, whatever the product's declared origin. That is a recommendation from an advocacy group, not policy.
India's Russian crude imports fell 13% in September, the second straight monthly decline and the lowest since April, CREA said. Intake dropped at all three of its largest importing refineries: Jamnagar by 27%, Indian Oil Corporation's (IOC) Paradip by 21% and Nayara Energy's Vadinar by 8%. "Despite the decline, Vadinar overtook Jamnagar as India's largest importer of Russian crude."
"India was the second-largest buyer of Russian fossil fuels in September 2026, importing a total of 4.1 billion euros of Russian hydrocarbons. Crude oil constituted 88% of India's purchases, totalling 3.6 billion euros. Coal (309 million euros) and oil products (161 million euros) constituted the remainder of its monthly Russian imports," CREA said.
Imports at smaller installations also mostly trended downwards, with the HMEL Mundra Oil Terminal and the Kochi refinery lowering intakes by 74% and 32%, respectively, month-on-month. "The main exception was the IOC Mundra Oil Terminal, which received 570 thousand tonnes of Russian crude in September after receiving none in August," CREA said.
India was Russia's second-largest fossil fuel customer in September, spending 4.1 billion euros on Russian hydrocarbons, 88% of it crude. Only China bought more. Since December 2022, India has taken 37% of Russia's crude exports, against China's 50%.
India was a marginal buyer of Russian oil before the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. It became a top customer as Western buyers retreated and Russia sold at steep discounts. Urals crude averaged $90.7 a barrel in September but still traded $23 below Brent, unchanged from August.
Analysts at Kpler say the fall in volumes partly reflects tighter supply and stronger Chinese competition for Russian barrels, not only U.S. pressure. They expect India's October imports to hold at 1.8-1.9 million barrels per day.

briefs.headline: PFRDA readies plan to onboard gig workers on National Pension System
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Lakhs of gig and platform workers may soon be able to plan for their retirement savings as Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) is working to open 
National Pension System
 (NPS) accounts for workers who are part of the e-shram database.
“Under the social security code, govt has to provide social security benefits to gig and platform workers. For the pension benefit, PFRDA suggested using the e-shramik model. We are tying up with the e-shram database now, will get a consent from the gig workers and open NPS accounts for them,” chairman S Raman told TOI in an interview.
These new accounts will be opened using the recently launched NPS Tatkal option, which allows subscribers to open accounts digitally and instantly through UPI-linked payment platforms, without requiring any paperwork.
The e-shramik model, which was launched in Oct 2025, enables both workers and aggregators to make flexible and micro-contributions -- as low as Rs 99 -- to the account without rigid monthly mandates. It is also linked to a Permanent Retirement Account Number (PRAN) so that a worker can access it anytime, irrespective of his or her employment or platform affiliation.
Utilising the e-shramik model is important as platforms have not been very forthcoming over the share and nature of contributions to be made by them towards social security benefits of workers. 
This provides them with a flexible option. For the gig and platform workers, this is beneficial as it allows them -- without regular earnings -- to start saving for retirement instead of deferring it.
“By default, these new accounts will follow the investment pattern of NPS Sanchaya. Afterwards, if the subscriber is interested to change their investment allocations, they will have the option to do so. This will allow them steady returns and build their savings over time,” said Raman.
NPS Sanchay follows a pre-defined, conservative-to-moderate investment pattern similar to govt sector NPS schemes. This is in contrast to regular NPS, where subscribers must actively choose the mix of investment between equities, corporate bonds, govt securities, and alternate assets.

briefs.headline: Bagchi to soon present HDFC Bank roadmap
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Anup Bagchi, who is set to take over as HDFC Bank’s managing director and CEO, said he would soon draw up a strategic roadmap covering growth, margins, asset quality and productivity, as outgoing chief Sashidhar Jagdishan said the bank’s net interest margins (NIMs) had bottomed out and would improve from the next quarter.
Speaking during the bank’s Q2 FY27 earnings call, Bagchi said he would consult regulators, customers, shareholders and other stakeholders before setting organisational priorities. He said the roadmap would focus on capital deployment, execution and governance as the bank responds to changes in the economy, artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure. “The clear long-term goal is to deliver sustainable long-term value for shareholders, employees, and clients,” Bagchi said.
Jagdishan, who is stepping down after six years at the helm, said margins had come under pressure because lending rates fell faster than the cost of deposits during the rate-cut cycle. He said the trend would reverse as the rate cycle turned and retail and MSME loans accounted for a larger share of the bank’s assets. “The trajectory will be upward from the next quarter on,” Jagdishan said, responding to a question on the outlook for margins.
HDFC Bank on Saturday reported a 4.7% year-on-year increase in net profit to 19,510 crore in the July-Sept quarter of FY27 (Q2FY27), as a decline in other income and higher operating expenses and provisions partly offset growth in core interest income.
With 70% of loans linked to floating rates, mostly to the repo, the Oct rate hike is expected to reprice much of the book by Dec. Of Rs 1.6 lakh crore in deposit growth, Rs 1.3 lakh crore came from time deposits and FCNR(B) inflows, offsetting gains from calling AT1 bonds in Aug.
Jagdishan said the branch network doubled over five years and will support deposit growth as it matures. Repayment of Rs 2.6 lakh crore in inherited HDFC Ltd wholesale borrowings distorted headline figures, while retail CASA remained in the late 40s. Technology investments are beginning to cut turnaround times through automated processes. Employee numbers have stayed flat for three years, but the workforce will shift towards customer-facing roles, with headcount potentially rising in three to four years.
Jagdishan announced that Bharucha, a 30-year veteran who helped build the bank’s credit architecture, had sought early retirement by Dec 31, 2026. Jagdishan also said his tenure had included regulatory restrictions, Covid, the HDFC Ltd merger and governance issues. Bagchi’s forthcoming roadmap will set the bank’s priorities under its new leadership.

briefs.headline: Finances for disabled
briefs.deck: Disability introduces a permanent, elevated baseline of living costs such as home retrofitting and full-time care-giving support
briefs.bodyText:
To sustain a life of dignity and independence, PwDs must pivot to calculated, aggressive investing.
Disability introduces a permanent, elevated baseline of living costs such as home retrofitting and full-time care-giving support. As per National Sample Survey 2018, out-of-pocket healthcare expenses for disability consume over 20% of an average household’s budget, rising past 30% for lower-income families.
Restricted earnings
Compounding these is a severely restricted earning potential. The public safety net offers little relief. Government welfare schemes are structured only as poverty alleviation steps than tools to sustain middle-class independence. While consumer inflation averages about 5-6%, healthcare inflation is between 11-13%, as per Aon and Milliman.
To survive the economic pressures, PwDs and families must adopt a high-growth, structured strategies:
-- Equity Mutual Funds: Equities are the primary accessible asset class in India capable of outpacing double-digit medical inflation. A disciplined systematic investment plan (SIP) or lumpsum investments in diversified equity MFs provides compounding mechanism to build a self-sustaining lifetime corpus.
-- Capitalizing tax provisions: Under Sec. 80U, certified PwDs can claim a flat deduction of ₹75,000 (for 40%-79% disability) or ₹1.25 lakh (severe disability). Caregivers of a dependent with a disability can claim deductions under Sec. 80DD in the old tax regime, freeing up capital for high-growth investments
-- Private health insurance: Despite waiting periods and premium loadings for pre-existing conditions, securing a private base health policy with high-deductible super top-up transfers catastrophic medical risks to an insurer.
-- High-cover term insurance: The family must secure a term life insurance policy where the PwD is the nominee and beneficiary. This guarantees an immediate, tax-free, high-value corpus on caregiver’s death, ensuring lifelong care funding without relying solely on accumulated savings.
-- Special Needs Trusts (SNTs): For individuals with severe intellectual disabilities, a private trust ensures the equity corpus is managed by trustees strictly for the beneficiary’s long-term care.
-- Assistive Tech : Where applicable, investing early in adaptive technology, accessible remote-work set-ups or vocational skills shifts the financial dynamic. Enabling gig-economy or remote work participation helps the individual to generate own income.
The combination of systemic inaccessibility, minimal social safety net and double-digit medical inflation gives rise to a hostile economic setting. In a system that does not support them, financial freedom turns the ultimate assistive technology. By investing aggressively and structuring wealth to outpace inflation, PwDs can secure the long-term autonomy and dignity the system denies them.
(The writer is founder - Rupee With Rushabh Investment Services www.rupeewithrushabh.com)

briefs.headline: What if a cheque bounces?
briefs.deck: The issuer must ensure sufficient balance when the cheque is presented and avoid issuing signed blank cheques
briefs.bodyText:
In this digital era, cash is gradually losing its sheen while digital payments are rising. Yet, in certain high-value transactions such as property purchases, business deals and loan repayments, cheque continues to hold its ground. A cheque is a bridge between a promise and a payment. When the bridge collapses, the promise is breached, money fails to reach its destination, giving rise to financial and legal consequences.
Let’s address some rudimentary aspects. To mitigate risk of disputes, both parties must verify the cheque’s particulars and check for errors or unauthorised alterations. The issuer must ensure sufficient balance when the cheque is presented and avoid issuing signed blank cheques.
However, a cheque may still be dishonoured by the bank, that is, payment may be refused and the cheque returned unpaid, a situation known as a cheque bounce. Generally, when a cheque bounces, the bank provides a return memo to the recipient stating the reason. The recipient must retain the memo and notify the issuer to resolve the payment issue. A cheque may bounce for several reasons, including insufficient funds, account closure, stop-payment instructions or signature mismatches. The legal consequences rest on reason for dishonour and circumstances.
Legal consequences
A cheque bounce may be treated as a criminal offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, punishable with imprisonment of up to two years, a fine of up to twice the cheque amount or both, if the statutory conditions are met.
Under Sections 118 and 139 of the Act, the court presumes, unless the contrary is proved, the cheque was issued for consideration and towards a legally enforceable debt or liability. The drawer (or accused) can rebut this by raising a probable defence that challenges the existence of the legally enforceable debt or liability.
For instance, Kamal issues Priya a cheque for ₹50,000 which is dishonoured due to insufficient funds. The court initially presumes Kamal owed Priya ₹50,000 and issued the cheque only to repay that debt. Kamal can challenge this by presenting evidence that casts doubt on the existence of his liability to Priya. However, he does not have to prove his case entirely on his own; the court considers proofs from both sides before arriving at a conclusion.
Legal timeline
The payee can initiate proceedings under Section 138 only if the cheque was presented within validity period, usually 3 months from its date. If the cheque bounced, the payee, within 30 days of receiving information from the bank, must send a written demand notice to the issuer. The defaulter has an option to settle the payment within 15 days from the date of receipt of the payee’s demand notice. If payment is not made within the stipulated time, the payee might file a written complaint before the competent Magistrate within a month (30 days) after the 15-day notice period expires.
The court may accept a late complaint if the complainant provides sufficient reason for the delay. The parties may also settle the case by mutual agreement as Section 147 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, permits such cases to be settled amicably. Further, the recipient may approach a civil court to recover the unpaid amount. For eligible claims, a summary suit offers a procedure to speed up the recovery of certain debts. Under the Limitation Act, 1963, a money-recovery claim usually must be filed within three years though the date from which this period begins depends on the nature of the claim.
(Dr. Sincy Wilson is an Assistant Professor of Law, Vels University (VISTAS). Dr. Vaishali R. Venkat is an NISM & CRISIL-certified Wealth Manager and certified in NISM’s Research Analyst module)
