briefs.headline: Your claim may be cashless, but not costless
briefs.deck: Cashless claim settlement promises a simpler way to handle hospitalisation insurance claims. But does it also promise freedom from hospital bills? Not quite.
briefs.bodyText:
Cashless. The word conjures up scenes of walking out of a hospital with a light step and a lighter heart. No bulky files, no submitting a claim and no chasing reimbursements. And certainly, no waiting anxiously. Yes?
Yes and no. Cashless is one of those words in insurance that have come to mean more than they mean or were ever meant to mean. Much more.
Introduced in the early 2000s, the cashless facility made use of growing technology to simplify and speed up hospitalisation claims. Documents could move electronically and, more crucially, the insurer could settle an admissible claim directly with the hospital instead of making the insured pay first and seek reimbursement later.
Alongside this grew an entire support industry: the Third-Party Administrator (Health Services), or TPAs. Insurers could and in the initial years were mandated to tie up with TPAs and outsource claim processing to them. This included receiving claim information, scrutinising documents and coordinating with hospitals, the insured and the insurer.
The decision on whether a claim was admissible and how much was payable was in the hands of the insurer, governed by the contract and the insurer’s claims process. Once decided, the insurer paid the hospital via TPA. In other words, cashless to insured.
But this is only the portion payable under the policy and this is the part those insured do not fully get, maybe partly due to the marketing cachet of the word ‘cashless’. Add to that the insured person’s belief that everything-under-the-sun-is-covered, and it easily became everything under the-sun is cashlessly-covered.
Every word matters
Every word in an insurance policy means something specific. Here, cashless only describes the mechanism for settling an admissible claim. Inadmissible claims or expense items in a hospital bill remain, well, inadmissible.
In a policy there is an annexure running into many pages listing expense items that are not covered. These could range from gloves to charges for medical records. If the hospital bills for these and your policy does not cover them, you have to pay.
Then there are the exclusions. Some expenses or treatments are excluded under the policy; others may not be covered during a specified waiting period.
Also not payable are portions of the claim that you have agreed to bear yourself, such as co-payments and deductibles.
If your policy has a room-rent limit, only the eligible room rent is admissible. If the hospital follows differential pricing based on room category, then choosing a higher room category may also lead to proportionate deductions from related expenses. And, any claim amount beyond the available sum insured is not payable.
Pre-authorisation
When you are admitted to a hospital, the hospital’s insurance or cashless desk will seek a pre-authorisation from the insurer or TPA. In an emergency or an accident, the timelines and process may work somewhat differently.
Say the hospital initially estimates the cost at ₹2 lakh and seeks authorisation for that amount. The insurer may pre-authorise ₹1.5 lakh. As treatment progresses, the hospital bill itself may rise beyond ₹2 lakh and further authorisation may be sought.
But what matters is the amount admissible under the policy viz. the amount that will be settled directly to the hospital. The balance is billed to you.
Not understanding this is why tempers fly high at the time of discharge. You thought you were walking away and the hospital wants you to pay ₹45,000.
Once you start questioning the bill, everybody becomes tight-faced. Front-office smoothness and deference rarely extends to the billing counter. Most often, patients and their families are too tired and low on morale after the health setback to argue. They pay up, or frantically try to arrange the money, simply so they can leave.
Some hospitals try to protect themselves against uncertainty over cashless settlement by asking patients for a sizeable deposit at admission, sometimes to cover what the policy will not pay but sometimes even the estimated treatment cost with the promise that whatever the insurer eventually settles will be returned to them.
That, my friends, is not cashless. In fact, it is the very opposite of it.
So, remember: cashless only removes the need for you to fund the insurer’s share of the bill. Your share of the bill is still very much yours.
(The writer is a business journalist specialising in insurance & corporate history.)

briefs.headline: Turtle Wax in India to grow 100% YoY in next 5 years, says global CEO, Laurie King
briefs.deck: Manufacturing locally is a key part of the company’s strategy to support expansion, stay closer to consumer base and reduce exposure to international freight costs and currency fluctuations
briefs.bodyText:
Turtle Wax, an American manufacturer of automotive appearance and car care products, expects India to become one of its largest markets worldwide over the next five years, riding on consecutive years of 100% year-on-year business growth.
Laurie King, Chief Executive Officer of Turtle Wax Inc in an exclusive conversation with The Hindu said, the company was stepping up its India expansion through a combination of domestic manufacturing, wider retail distribution, technology-led products and services catering to both do-it-yourself (DIY) consumers and professional detailing studios.
``Since we started operations here in 2019, our business has doubled year over year, and we expect that momentum to continue,’’ Ms. King said in Bengaluru. She said rising automobile ownership and growing consumer interest in vehicle maintenance offered considerable room for expansion.
The 80-year-old US-headquartered company, originally founded in 1941 by Benjamin Hirsch in Chicago, Illinois, operates in more than 130 countries, with established markets in North America, Europe, the Middle East, Southeast Asia and China. While the US remains its largest market, India is emerging as a significant growth opportunity.
Turtle Wax currently has more than 110 Car Care Studios across India, operating through a co-branded model in partnership with independent detailing entrepreneurs. The company plans to add over 50 studios in the next year, supported by technician training through its Detailing Academy, a training institute that teaches people how to professionally clean, restore, and protect cars and bikes.
Ms. King said the academy helped standardise application techniques, safety practices and customer service across the network, enabling the company to maintain consistent service quality in a fragmented market.
Focus on starting manufacturing in India
According to her, domestic manufacturing is a key part of the company’s strategy to support expansion and reduce exposure to international freight costs and currency fluctuations. Ms. King said Turtle Wax had begun taking concrete steps towards local production and was continuing to scale these efforts.
``Producing closer to our consumer base helps insulate us from global shipping costs and currency shifts, while drastically shortening turnaround times,’’ she said.
The move comes amid volatility in global trade routes and supply chains. The company is also diversifying sourcing and production across North America, Europe and Asia, while maintaining strategic buffer stocks to minimise disruptions and ensure supplies to retail partners and studios.
On the DIY front, Turtle Wax is seeking to broaden its reach beyond metropolitan markets by offering products across price and performance categories, from basic vehicle maintenance to advanced ceramic protection. Its newer product, Pure Bead, uses a formulation designed to create a tight molecular bond that helps water and road grime slide off vehicle surfaces, simplifying cleaning in challenging weather conditions, as per her.
Ms. King said Indian conditions, including intense sunlight, monsoon rains and fine dust, required products suited to local vehicle-care needs. The company was focusing on formulations that offer effective protection without complicated application processes, particularly for consumers in Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities, she said.
The DIY segment was also gaining traction in India as consumers increasingly used e-commerce platforms, online reviews and video demonstrations to research car care products. ``Car care in India was increasingly becoming an experiential activity rather than a routine chore, with consumers seeking to preserve the showroom appearance of their vehicles,’’ Ms. King observed.
Globally, she added, the car care industry was moving towards greater efficiency and reduced water consumption. ``Our challenge in India to translate India’s fast-growing interest in vehicle care into sustained business growth,’’ Ms. King concluded.

Babar Azam

Babar entered the match with 15,993 runs and needed seven more to reach the 16,000-run mark. He achieved the feat in the fourth over of the day, having come out to bat after Saim Ayub was dismissed by Dilshan Madushanka.  holds the world record for the most runs in international cricket. He scored 34,357 runs during his career, which spanned from 1989 to 2013.

Manasi Joshi and Thulasimathi Murugesan assured India of a medal for the second successive edition, securing a semifinal berth in women's doubles SL3-SU5 at the Asian Para Games here on Saturday (October 17, 2026).

stories.headline: Amruta wins silver as Indian women end U23 Worlds with two medals
stories.deck: Amruta was trailing 0-6 when Zablotska managed a decisive pin to seal the gold medal
stories.bodyText:
Amruta Pujari settled for a silver medal after losing the women's 72kg final 'by fall' to Ukraine's Iryna Zablotska, as Indian women concluded their campaign with two medals at the U23 World Wrestling Championships.
Amruta was trailing 0-6 when Zablotska managed a decisive pin to seal the gold medal.
India's Sweety came close to adding another medal but lost the 53kg bronze medal play-off by technical superiority (0-11) to Ukraine's Anastasiia Polska.
Sweety had reached the bronze medal bout after edging past China's Xiaotong Zeng 11-10 in the repechage round.
Vaishnavi Patil, however, failed to capitalise on her repechage opportunity, going down 2-4 to Japan's Haruka Kobaru.
Komal had earlier won a bronze medal in the women's 59kg weight category.
The Indian men's freestyle wrestlers, meanwhile, endured a disappointing campaign with none of the five competitors in action managing to reach the medal rounds on Friday.
Vaibhav Patil was knocked out of the 61kg competition after losing his pre-quarterfinal bout by technical superiority (0-11) to Romania's Gabriel Whisenhunt.
In the 74kg category, Adarsh Patil bowed out following a 4-6 defeat to Japan's Toki Ogawal in the round of 16.
Amit's campaign in the 86kg division also ended in the round of 16. He lost by fall to Georgia's Tornike Samkharadze while trailing 3-4.
Nikhil suffered a similar fate in the 92kg category, losing his round-of-16 bout by technical superiority to Georgia's Sandro Kurashvili.
In the heavyweight 125kg division, Ronak Dahya exited after losing his quarterfinal bout by technical superiority (1-11) to Azerbaijan's Khetag Karsanov.
In a below par show, India have so far won just three medals in the tournament with Greco Roman wrestler Vishvajit More winning a silver in the 55kg division.

briefs.headline: Jaskaran, Chandermohan enter bronze medal bouts at U23 Worlds
briefs.deck: Competing in the 65kg freestyle category, Jaskaran registered two technical superiority wins before edging past American wrestler Bowen William Bassett 6-3 in the quarterfinals
briefs.bodyText:
Jaskaran Singh and Chandermohan entered the bronze medal bouts in their respective weight categories, while Rohit and Shivan remained in contention through the repechage at the U23 World Wrestling Championships in Las Vegas.
Competing in the 65kg freestyle category, Jaskaran registered two technical superiority wins before edging past American wrestler Bowen William Bassett 6-3 in the quarterfinals.
However, he failed to make the final after losing his semifinal bout by technical superiority to Japan's Kaiji Ogino, leaving him to fight for a bronze medal.
Chandermohan also made it to the bronze medal bout in the 79kg category after an impressive run to the semifinals.
He began with a 14-4 win over Georgia's Giorgi Gogritchiani before blanking Brazil's Kydyn Luk Correa Lima 14-0. He then recorded another technical superiority victory, beating American Joseph Lee Sealey 11-0.
However, Chandermohan narrowly missed out on a place in the final, losing his semifinal 3-4 to Iran's Mahdi Mohammad Yousefihajivar.
In the 57kg category, Rohit began his campaign with a technical superiority win over Jamaica's Irie Alexander Jackson but suffered a 6-10 defeat to Turkiye's Bekir Keser in the pre-quarterfinals.
He kept his medal hopes alive by progressing through the repechage and is scheduled to face Moldova's Ion Bulgaru.
Shivam also remained in the medal race in the 97kg category through the repechage route.
However, Sumit Bharaskar's campaign ended in the 70kg category, with the Indian failing to remain in contention for a medal.

briefs.headline: Chwalinska fights back to win Wuhan Open in title breakthrough
briefs.deck: The Polish 16th seed trailed by a set and a break before she turned things around to become just the fourth player to win her maiden tour-level title at a WTA 1000 event
briefs.bodyText:
Maja Chwalinska pulled off an impressive comeback to defeat Britain's Sonay Kartal 2-6, 6-4, 6-2 and claim the first tour-level title of her career at the Wuhan Open on Sunday (October 18, 2026).
The Polish 16th seed trailed by a set and a break before she turned things around to become just the fourth player to win her maiden tour-level title at a WTA 1000 event.
She joins Naomi Osaka (2018 Indian Wells), Bianca Andreescu (2019 Indian Wells) and Victoria Mboko (2025 Montreal) in that exclusive club.
The 25-year-old Chwalinska started the year ranked 146 in the world and provided one of the biggest surprises of the season when she reached the French Open final as a qualifier in June.
"(This title) tastes very sweet. I feel like I still don't realise that I won," Chwalinska said in the post-match press conference.
"But it feels special, because after French Open, it was obviously amazing, but then I had some tough moments. I feel like people also were very rough towards me. And it took a toll on me as well.
"I'm just a human. But I kept working really hard and I'm just very grateful that my work paid off."
The talented lefty will now rise to a career-high No.11 in the world, making her top-20 debut when the new rankings are released on Monday (October 19).
"I feel like my energy level was very low at the beginning, but also Sonay played amazing," added Chwalinska.
"Gradually I started to play much better and much more aggressive. Also, the depth on my shots improved.
"I feel what I'm proud of is the fighting spirit that I had. I just wanted to fight for every single ball and hoped that things would click at some point."
Kartal, who was contesting her second tour event back from a six-month hiatus due to a spinal stress fracture, entered Wuhan ranked 170 in the world but will return to the top 50 after reaching the first WTA 1000 final of her career.
'Head high'
The first set was one-way traffic, with Kartal dictating play with heavy hitting from the baseline and Chwalinska scrambling to defend from all corners of the court.
It took three breaks of serve and 45 minutes to give Kartal a one-set lead and send her closer to the biggest title of her career.
Chwalinska found her legs in the second set and began to put pressure on the Kartal serve by employing the methods that helped her knock out her compatriot Iga Swiatek in the semi-finals: extending the rallies, running down every ball, and mixing things up with her smooth touch.
Despite saving 10 out of 13 break points and holding a 2-0 advantage early in the frame, Kartal surrendered the second set after 71 minutes.
Kartal ran out of steam in the decider as Chwalinska broke twice to secure the trophy on her third championship point after a gruelling two hours and 43 minutes.
"It was a very physical battle and I think I had my chances and I think that's maybe where the rust of six months off comes in," said Kartal.
"But overall I'm very happy with my performance. Obviously not the result I wanted and it's going to sting for a little while but I think for me the positives this week outweigh that result today. So yeah I'm leaving here head out high and in a good spot overall."

briefs.headline: India's Para Asian Games contingent showcases 5,000 years of heritage
briefs.deck: More than 100 Indian athletes took part in the ceremony, led by Paralympic medallist sprinter Simran Sharma and top shuttler Pramod Bhagat, who carried the national flag as the contingent marched in with the Tricolour fluttering proudly
briefs.bodyText:
The Indian contingent brought a touch of the country's rich heritage to the opening ceremony of the Para Asian Games on Sunday (October 19, 2026), with athletes donning ceremonial blazers featuring motifs inspired by 5,000 years of civilisation.
More than 100 Indian athletes took part in the ceremony, led by Paralympic medallist sprinter Simran Sharma and top shuttler Pramod Bhagat, who carried the national flag as the contingent marched in with the Tricolour fluttering proudly.
The ceremonial blazers featured prints of seals from the Indus Valley, drawing on the ancient script and motifs of one of the world’s oldest civilisations.
“Team India walked out wearing more than just ceremonial dress — they wore 5,000 years of civilisation. The Indian contingent’s ceremonial blazer is a tribute to our heritage,” the Paralympic Committee of India said.
The blazers also featured SaptSindhu on the collar, honouring the land of the seven rivers and the mighty Saraswati, while the Tricolour was placed prominently on the pocket.
India is fielding a 281-member contingent, comprising 168 athletes — 112 men and 56 women — competing across 11 disciplines.
The Games will conclude on October 24, with around 3,000 athletes from 45 nations competing under the motto "Imagine One Heart".
India enjoyed its most successful Asian Para Games campaign in Hangzhou in 2023, finishing fifth in the medal standings with a record haul of 111 medals — 29 gold, 31 silver and 51 bronze.

briefs.headline: Agha's comeback century sinks Sri Lanka and gives Pakistan winning start in tri-series
briefs.deck: Agha hit 107 off 90 balls, and Pakistan scored 305 all out in 49.5 overs after Sri Lanka captain Kusal Mendis won his fourth successive toss and chose to field
briefs.bodyText:
Salman Ali Agha made a triumphant return to the Pakistan team with his fourth ODI century in a 37-run victory over Sri Lanka in the cricket tri-series opener on Sunday (October 18, 2026).
Agha hit 107 off 90 balls, and Pakistan scored 305 all out in 49.5 overs after Sri Lanka captain Kusal Mendis won his fourth successive toss and chose to field.
Agha was among seven Pakistan cricketers summoned back home at the end of August during a tumultuous tour of England after Agha had led the team in the first test.
Pakistan pace bowlers overcame heavy dew and threatening half centuries from Pavan Rathnayake (79) and Janith Liyanage (60) to dismiss Sri Lanka for 268 in 48.1 overs.
Captain Shaheen Afridi picked up 3-55 while Naseem Shah pinned down Sri Lanka's top-order with impressive swing bowling to finish with 2-43. Haris Rauf ran through the tail with 2-48 while seam all-rounder Faheem Ashraf grabbed 2-49, including the key wicket of Rathnayake.
Pakistan will play England in Rawalpindi on Tuesday (October 20) in the second match of the tri-series.
Sri Lanka struggles against paceAvishka Fernando, making a comeback to ODIs, top-edged Shah while Kusal Mendis struggled for 34 balls to score only 18 before he fell to Ashraf.
Kamindu Mendis (44 in 50) survived two dropped catches before Afridi struck twice in his return spell as Sri Lanka limped to 91-4 in the 20th over of its chase.
Rathnayake and Liyanage then revived Sri Lankan hopes with a 119-run stand with Pakistan pacers unable to reverse swing the wet ball due to heavy dew at Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium. But the dismissal of Rathnayake in the 38th over provided Pakistan an opening despite Dasun Shanaka, playing his first ODI since the start of 2024, scoring 28 off 18 balls.
Agha revives Pakistan
After being summoned home, Agha was later not only removed as Pakistan T20 captain but also lost his place in the T20 team that beat Sri Lanka 2-1 in the recent three-match series. However, Agha scored prolifically in domestic cricket, including a triple century and forced his way back into the ODI side.
Agha revived Pakistan from 118-4 in the 22nd over with partnerships with Hasan Nawaz (37) and Arafat Minhas (18) before Sri Lanka hit back in the death overs.
Eshan Malinga (4-46) and Asitha Fernando (3-59) denied Pakistan a big finish in the final five overs with multiple strikes as Pakistan, at 279-5, went on to lose its last five wickets for 26 runs. Malinga bowled a double-wicket maiden over before No. 11 Haris Rauf denied him a hat trick.
Dilshan Madushanka (2-67) removed openers Fakhar Zaman (16) and Saim Ayub (7) in his opening spell.
Babar Azam and 19-year-old debutant Saad Baig rebuilt with a 74-run third-wicket stand before Malinga removed both batters in successive overs.
Babar, who has scored just one ODI hundred in more than two years, fell for 45 off 57 balls when he pulled Malinga's short ball to mid-wicket. Baig smashed two sixes and three fours before he too was tempted to pull Malinga and holed out at deep fine leg.
Agha snatched the momentum from Sri Lanka with a 97-run stand with Nawaz. The only specialist leg-spinner Sachindu Colombage (0-61) struggled as Agha completed his half century off 48 balls and Nawaz also opened up against the leg-spinner.
Fernando returned and broke the partnership when Nawaz was well caught by Rathnayake over his head at mid-wicket. Agha continued to bat aggressively in a 64-run stand with Minhas before raising his hundred with an edged boundary.

briefs.headline: Shafali, Mandhana shine as India beat Zimbabwe by 9 wickets to take unassailable 2-0 series lead
briefs.deck: Shafali and skipper Smriti Mandhana (47 not out) unfurled their elite skills to decimate the tourists during their riveting opening stand, as India chased down the target of 103 in a mere 8.5 overs
briefs.bodyText:
Opener Shafali Verma clobbered a 25-ball 55 as India dismantled an inexperienced Zimbabwe by nine wickets in the second women’s T20I to take an unassailable 2-0 lead in the three-match series here on Sunday (October 18, 2026).
The result of the match was a forgone conclusion once Zimbabwe were restricted to a lowly 102 for eight after they opted to bat first.
Shafali and skipper Smriti Mandhana (47 not out) unfurled their elite skills to decimate the tourists during their riveting opening stand, as India chased down the target of 103 in a mere 8.5 overs.
It also helped Mandhana begin her full-time captaincy stint with a series triumph.
Shafali, who added 96 runs with Mandhana, reached her fifty in 26 balls by hitting off-spinner Beloved Biza for a six. It was her 22nd half-century in T20Is.
Michelle Mavunga suffered at the hands of the Indian opener, getting creamed for 4, 4, 6 in successive balls.
Mandhana too had her moments when she peeled off four boundaries in a row off pacer Nyasha Gwanzura, indicating her touch on the day.
She applied finishing touches to the match with an excellent inside out six off Olinder Chare.
Earlier, Indian bowlers produced a wonderful collective effort to restrict Zimbabwe to a lowly total.
Once they elected to bat first, Zimbabwe never really managed to impart momentum to their innings at any stage.
Pacer Nandani Sharma castled opener Kelis Ndhlovu for an 11-ball duck as the African side could not get off to a strong start.
All they could manage was just 20 runs in the Power Play segment for the loss of Ndhlovu. In fact, the tourists managed just one boundary in that period, that came off the last ball of the Power Play.
Biza too departed two balls after the Power Play, piling more pressure on the Zimbabweans.
Skipper Josephine Nkomo (27 not out) and Chipo Tiripano (34, 32 balls) then added 45 runs for the fourth wicket and that turned out to be the best part of their innings.
Tiripano, who received reprieves on 20 and 22, looked solid, and even creamed premier left-arm spinner Shree Charani for two reverse-swept fours in a row.
The partnership saw Zimbabweans fetch seven boundaries, trying to keep going. It helped the visitors add 56 runs in the middle phase from overs 7 to 15.
But off-spinner Niki Prasad (2/7) broke the partnership, eliciting an edge from Tiripano for stumper Richa Ghosh to take an easy catch.
Niki trapped Nyasha Gwanzura in front of the wicket to place herself near a hat-trick but could not achieve the rare feat.
But that hardly mattered as India by then had taken complete control of the proceedings.
